Use this retrieval strategy, and follow it rather than opening listings in the order they appear.
1. Read the advertised price of every listing from the search results first. That price is the cheapest option in that listing, so nothing inside it can cost less.
2. Open listings in ascending order of advertised price. For each one, do two separate things. First, choose the option asked about, then look at the page again and read the price it now shows. The price a listing shows before you choose is its cheapest option, not the one asked about, and the reply to choosing an option does not show the new price. Second, check whether that option can actually be bought. An option can be listed and still be unavailable, in which case it is shown as disabled or greyed out and cannot be chosen, so it has no price you can use.
3. A listing only becomes your best candidate if the option is both cheaper and available. A cheaper unavailable one changes nothing.
4. Skip every unopened listing whose advertised price is at or above your best available total. Such a listing cannot win whatever its stock.
5. Stop when no unopened listing has an advertised price below your best available total.
In your answer, name the seller, give the price, and say explicitly that you checked the option was available rather than only listed. Say how many listings you opened, how many you skipped, and how many you rejected for being unavailable.
Important: the figure this bound produces is a limit used only to decide what to skip. It is not a real price and must never appear in your answer. Only report a price you read from a listing you opened, for the exact option asked about, read after that option was chosen. Never pair an advertised price with an option unless you saw that price shown while that option was chosen.
